tone_statements.citation: Odden, David (with the assistance of Deogratius Tungaraza). n.d. [c. 2006]. Kikerewe-English Dictionary. Preliminary draft. Columbus: Department of Linguistics, Ohio State University. Front matter 'Orthography' (tone and vowel length), pp. i-iv. the Internet Archive copy ofhttp://ling.ohio-state.edu/~odden/kerewedic.pdf(capture 2006-09-05).
tone_statements.quote: Kikerewe also makes distinctive use of tones. The unmarked or basic tone is low tone, which is indicated with no accent on a vowel. The marked or special tone is high tone raised pitch , marked with an accute accent. ikala civet ika¬la charcoal kubala to count kuba¬la to kick … In a few rare instances within the lexicon, two H toned syllables may be next to each other, … In such a case, the symbol ! is used to mark exceptional lowering of the second syllables H tone known as downstep
tone_statements.locator: Front matter 'Orthography', tone and vowel length paragraphs, pp. iii-iv

sources.citation: Odden, David (with Deogratius Tungaraza). n.d. [c. 2006]. Kikerewe-English Dictionary. Preliminary draft. Columbus: Ohio State University. Front matter pp. i-vii.
sources.note: Orthography/tone/vowel-length section (pp. i-iv) states that Kikerewe makes distinctive use of vowel length and of tone (privative H vs. unmarked low; downstep), with minimal pairs; nothing said about stress or penultimate prominence. Obtained from the the Internet Archive copy of Odden's old OSU page (capture 2006-09-05).

sources.citation: Thornell, Christina. 2002. A preliminary sketch of time, aspect and mood in Kikerebe. Africa & Asia (Göteborg) 2: 125-147.
sources.note: No phonology section; tone is named only as a topic for future research (pp. 126, 146); stress not mentioned. Cites Hurel 1909 for the tense division.

sources.citation: Hurel, Eugène. 1909. La langue kikerewe: essai de grammaire. Mitteilungen des Seminars für Orientalische Sprachen 12, III. Abt. (Afrikanische Studien), 1-113.
sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent tonique. 'Préliminaires' (pp. 2-4) give only the alphabet, vowel length and euphony rules. p. 3: 'Il est très important dans la prononciation de faire longues ou brèves, selon le cas, les voyelles a, e, i, o, u, car souvent une inattention sur ce point change le sens des mots et fait qu'on n'est pas compris. Ex.: ku-nāra (a long) veut dire: uriner. ku-nara (a bref) veut dire: souffrir, peiner.' p. 2 (letter L): 'L = l s'emploie quelquefois indifféremment avec r.. mais sert dans l'accentuation des mots en ce sens que le l rendrait brève la voyelle qui suit, tandis…

sources.citation: Odden, David. 2015. Bantu phonology. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics (author preprint, 33 pp.).
sources.note: Kerewe cited for h/p, glide formation/hiatus and Tone Doubling; no statement about Kerewe stress (the only 'antepenult/penult' passage concerns Xhosa).

sources.citation: Odden, David. n.d. [c. 2005]. Ordering. Ms., Ohio State University (OT/opacity paper built on Kikerewe tone; published as Odden 2000, Opacity and ordering: H-deletion in Kikerewe, The Linguistic Review 17: 323-335).
sources.note: Detailed Kikerewe tone facts (Tone Doubling, final H shifting to the penult, 'Utterance-penult long vowels', penult H realised as fall on a long penult when underlying, level when shifted). 'Stress' appears only for Makonde and Bedouin Arabic; no Kikerewe stress statement.

sources.citation: Odden, David. 1996. Patterns of reduplication in Kikerewe. OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 48: 111-148.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Notes phrase-level lengthening before NC (word-final long vowels in endaláá ndéehi 'tall leopard', fn.) and melodic H assigned to the penultimate syllable in the near future tense; all prominence discussed is tonal.

sources.citation: Odden, David. 1995. The status of onsetless syllables in Kikerewe. OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 47: 89-110.
sources.note: Syllable structure, vowel length (compensatory lengthening, NC lengthening) and tone; privative H/toneless contrast (fn.); 'any H tone in the language spreads one syllable to the right, unless that H tone is in the phrasal penult' (p. 97). The word 'stress' occurs only in citations of other work; no statement about Kikerewe stress.

sources.citation: Odden, David. n.d. Kikerewe Tone (course problem set, Introducing Phonology).
sources.note: Tone data only (H doubling, phrasal penult); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Odden, David. 2022. Radical substance-free phonology and feature learning. Canadian Journal of Linguistics/Revue canadienne de linguistique 67(4): 500-551. Cambridge University Press.
sources.quote: Besides these obvious segmental distinctions, Kerewe is a tone language, but tonal properties are not analyzed here.
sources.locator: Section 4.2 'Acquisition of Kerewe features', sentence following the segment inventory
sources.note: A theoretical feature-learning paper whose empirical core (sec. 4.2) is an analysis of Kerewe segmental phonology (segment inventory, vowel length contrast, segmental rules). It states first-hand that Kerewe is a tone language but explicitly sets tone aside ('tonal properties are not analyzed here'); footnote 49 adds that Kerewe syllabification is motivated by facts of vowel length, tone and reduplication. No tone inventory or tonal rules given.
